newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan premium widens on DKB fund demand.
newsitem.headline: Japan premium widens on DKB fund demand.

text.p: The Japan premium -- the extra cost Japanese banks pay for raising funds in the eurodollar interbank market -- has widened as scandal-hit Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) struggles to ensure long-term liquidity beyond September, traders said on Tuesday.

On Tuesday, a few Japanese banks, including DKB, were paying a premium of 5/32 of a point for one-month eurodollar deposits over the rate of 5-20/32 percent for major European and U.S. banks with better credit ratings, traders said.
The premium was 4/32 of a point a week ago, they said.

DKB's persistent demand for funds was thought to reflect a desire to raise ample funds to cover interim book closings at the end of September, although the bank is not facing an imminent liquidity crunch, traders said.
DKB has also been active in raising funds in the short-term yen money market, they said.

Meanwhile, DKB has been shrinking its proprietary dealing positions and other areas of exposure in the short-term market, and possibly in Japanese government bonds and currencies as well, traders added.
The premium at one point jumped to 8/32 of a point on May 20 when prosecutors raided DKB's headquarters for the first time.

Prosecutors on Friday arrested DKB vice president Ichiro Fujita and another executive on suspicion of making illegal loans to a racketeer, bringing to 10 the number of DKB officials arrested in connection with the payoff scandal.
